A college founded at Aligarh in northern India in 1875 by the reformer Syed Ahmad Khan to give Indian Muslims a modern Western education. It began as a school and became the Muhammadan Anglo-Oriental College in 1877, and in 1920 Aligarh Muslim University.

After the Indian Rebellion of 1857, the old Muslim elite of north India had lost power and many shunned English schooling. Syed Ahmad believed Muslims must learn science and English to recover, and that Islam and reason did not conflict. He modelled the college on Oxford and Cambridge, with residential halls, sport and teaching in English alongside Islamic studies.

Its graduates formed a new Muslim professional and political class, the core of the "Aligarh movement". They were prominent in founding the All-India Muslim League in 1906 and later in the movement for Pakistan, led by Jinnah. A rival approach to Muslim renewal came from the traditional seminary of Deoband. The university remains one of India's major universities.
